notes.meaning: The Passover season was approaching in Jerusalem. The ancient feast of Passover and the seven-day Feast of Unleavened Bread were celebrated together as one holiday. Crowds were filling the city, setting the stage for what God had planned from the beginning.

The chief priests and teachers of the law wanted to put Jesus to death, but they were afraid of the crowds. Many ordinary people respected Jesus and listened eagerly to His preaching. The leaders knew an open arrest might cause a riot, so they searched for a quiet, cunning way to take Him.

Satan entered into Judas, one of Jesus' twelve closest followers. Judas had opened his heart to greed and selfish thoughts, giving the devil an opportunity to influence him. Even though Satan urged him on, Judas remained entirely responsible for his own evil choice.

Judas slipped away to talk with the leading priests and temple guards about handing Jesus over to them. The leaders needed an insider who knew where Jesus spent time alone. Treachery from someone who pretends to be a friend often causes great harm to God's people.

The religious rulers were glad that one of Jesus' own disciples came forward to help them. They made an agreement to pay him a sum of money. Judas let the love of money drive him into an awful betrayal.

Judas accepted their offer and began looking for a good chance to hand Jesus over. He needed a time when no crowds were nearby to protect Jesus or cause an uproar. Even through this wicked scheme, God was moving events toward His appointed time for Christ's sacrifice.

The day arrived when the Passover lamb had to be sacrificed according to the law of Moses. This annual meal remembered how God rescued Israel from slavery in Egypt. Jesus was now preparing to offer Himself as the true sacrifice to free people from sin.

Jesus chose Peter and John and sent them to get the Passover meal ready. This involved finding a room, securing the food, and preparing everything according to the law. Jesus carefully kept God's ordinances even as His earthly life drew to a close.
The disciples asked Jesus where He wanted them to make the preparations. Finding an open room in a crowded city full of pilgrims was not simple. They relied on their Master to direct their steps.

Jesus gave them an unusual sign, telling them they would meet a man carrying a water jug when they entered the city. Carrying water jars was normally women's work, so this man would easily stand out. Jesus showed that He knew every detail in advance and was in complete control.

Jesus told them to ask the owner of the house for the guest room where the Teacher could eat with His disciples. Calling Himself the Teacher carried quiet authority and showed that the homeowner likely knew Him. Keeping the location secret beforehand also kept Judas from interfering before the meal took place.

The man would take them upstairs to a large room that was already swept and furnished with dining couches. Jesus assured them that the space was ready for use. The two disciples only needed to follow His directions and prepare the food.

Peter and John went into the city and found everything just as Jesus had promised. Those who follow Christ's word never find His promises lacking. They got the lamb, bitter herbs, and bread ready for the holy feast.

When the evening arrived, Jesus reclined at the table with His twelve apostles. Reclining on low couches was the ordinary posture for a sacred banquet in those days. Even though His final trial was near, Jesus gathered His closest friends for fellowship.

Jesus told the disciples that He had deeply longed to eat this Passover with them before He suffered. He knew His death was at hand, yet He welcomed it because it would bring glory to God and rescue sinners. He also wanted this final private moment to comfort and prepare His followers.

Jesus said He would not eat the Passover again until its true meaning was fulfilled in the kingdom of God. The old feast was a picture that pointed ahead to Christ's sacrifice on the cross. Its ultimate fulfillment will be celebrated at the great heavenly banquet with all of God's redeemed people.

Jesus took a cup of wine used during the Passover meal, gave thanks to God, and told the disciples to share it among themselves. The traditional Jewish supper included several cups of wine taken at different points. By sharing this cup, Jesus was bringing the old ceremonial rites to their end.

Jesus declared that He would not drink wine again until the kingdom of God arrived. His earthly ministry of table fellowship was coming to a close. His death the very next day would begin the gospel age and open the way to God's kingdom.

Jesus took bread, gave thanks to God, broke it into pieces, and handed it to His disciples. He explained that this bread represented His body, which was given on the cross in their place to pay for sin, making an atonement. He told them to keep repeating this meal in remembrance of Him and His sacrifice.

differ.view: Christ's true physical body and blood are present in, with, and under the bread and wine for believers to receive.
Christ is truly present in the Lord's Supper, but spiritually rather than physically, feeding believers as they take the elements in faith.
The bread and wine are symbols that represent Christ's body and blood, taken as a memorial of His death.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The bread and wine are transformed into the actual body and blood of Christ, and His command to 'do this' ordained the apostles as priests to offer the sacrifice of the Mass.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars note that several ancient manuscripts omit verses 19b through 20, leading them to suggest that this sacrificial wording may have been added later from Paul's writings.

notes.meaning: After supper, Jesus lifted the cup and established the new covenant in His blood, which was poured out for them. A covenant is a sacred bond between God and His people, and this new agreement was sealed with Christ's own blood shed on the cross. The cup assures believers that their sins are forgiven and God's promises are secure.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: A number of scholars view this verse as part of a later addition because certain early manuscripts leave out verses 19b–20 entirely and describe only one cup before the bread.

notes.meaning: Jesus startled the disciples by saying that His betrayer was sitting right there with Him at the table. In ancient culture, sharing a meal was a sign of close friendship and loyalty, making Judas's action even more shocking. Jesus showed that nothing was hidden from Him and that He knew what was happening.

Jesus was going to His death exactly as God had determined in Scripture, but terrible judgment waited for the man who betrayed Him. God's plan did not force Judas to sin or take away his guilt. The traitor acted freely out of his own wicked heart and remained fully accountable.

The disciples began to question each other, wondering which of them could ever do such a terrible thing. Judas had hidden his deceit so well that the others did not suspect him. Distressed by Jesus' words, each man wondered about his own heart and the loyalty of the others.

An argument broke out among the disciples about which one of them should be regarded as the greatest. They were still expecting Jesus to set up an earthly kingdom where they would receive high rank and titles. It was shameful that they were arguing over worldly greatness right as their Master was preparing to lay down His life.
